Part 1 · Fundamentals

Why does acetone leave the water for TCE, and how far can it go?

Part 1 · the plan

From one drop of solvent to a whole cascade

  1. Three components, two liquid phaseswho is carrier, solute and solvent, and why TCE
  2. The ternary diagramwhere the mixture splits, and how temperature moves the split
  3. Mixing point and lever rulewhat one equilibrium stage can and cannot do
  4. Counter-current stagesoperating line, McCabe–Thiele steps and the Kremser equation
  5. Minimum solventthe least TCE that can ever reach the target

Three components

Who is who in this extraction

A · carrier

Water. It brings the acetone in.

B · solute

Acetone, 45 wt% of the feed.

C · solvent

TCE, barely mixes with water.

Extract (E)

Solvent-rich phase leaving with most acetone.

Raffinate (R)

Carrier-rich phase left behind.

Solubility in the other phase~0.4 wt%~0.1 wt%little solvent lost

Mutual solubilities are the OTS model values at 25 °C.

The ternary diagram

The dome and its tie linesstep 2 of 2

  • Inside the binodal curve (dome) a mixture splits into two liquids.
  • A tie line joins the two phases in equilibrium.
  • Tie lines tilt toward TCE: acetone prefers the solvent.
  • At the plait point the two phases become identical.

Interactive · pick a temperature

How temperature moves the two-liquid region

Brown squares: measured tie lines at 25 °C (book fig 6-65). Other temperatures: model predictions.

Warming stretches the dome toward the acetone corner and raises KD′​: on equilibrium alone, a warmer column extracts better.

How much can one mixer-settler do?

Lever ruleE/M=MR/ER

One stage with 350 kg/h leaves about 30 wt% acetone (SF); reaching 10 wt% in one stage needs about four times the solvent.

Many stages

Counter-current flow reuses the solvent

One stage wastes solvent. Passing the phases against each other through N stages fixes that.

In the RDC the stages are not separate boxes: height plays their part (Part 2).

Kremser, with numbers

How many stages does 10 wt% need?

From the previous slideXF​XR,N​​=EN+1−1E−1​,E=FA​KD′​SC​​
E=1.85×350/550=1.18design flows, 25 °C

Book: about 4 stages (triangle), 5 (McCabe–Thiele).

The least solvent that can work

Minimum solvent: a pinch at the feed end

EquilibriumXE​=KD′​XR​
XE,1​→KD′​XF​infinite stages: extract meets fresh feed in equilibrium
SC,min​=KD′​XF​FA​(XF​−XR,N​)​overall acetone balance at that limit
SC,min​=1.85×0.818550(0.818−0.111)​=257 kg/hbook: 257 algebraic, 265 graphical

Design 350 kg/h is 1.36 × minimum, inside the usual 1.3–1.5.

Part 1 · summary

What Part 1 settled

  • Acetone splits between water and TCE along tie lines; KD′​=1.85 at 25 °C.
  • One stage leaves about 30 wt% acetone (SF); counter-current stages reach 10 wt%.
  • Kremser: about 4 stages at S/F 0.35; minimum solvent 257 kg/h.
  • Warmer raises KD′​; the hydraulics, not equilibrium, set the temperature (Part 3).

What is inside an RDC

Each rotor disc and stator ring forms one compartment: the discs make drops, the rings stop the liquid short-circuiting.

Density889 kg/m³1435 kg/m³

Disperse the smaller volume flow. Heavy drops fall, so the interface sits in the bottom settler.

Interactive · sizing the height

How tall for a target?

Kremser and heightN from E and target; H=N×HETS

Halving the target to 5 wt% adds about 70 % more height: the last acetone is the most expensive to remove.

The two ends of the column

Settlers let the phases part

  • Top settler: drops disengage; clear raffinate leaves.
  • Bottom settler: drops coalesce into the extract layer.
  • The interface between them is held at 50 % by LIC-109.
  • An emulsion band sits on the interface; fine drops thicken it.

What came from where

The design basis of the OTS column

From the lecture notesAssumed for the OTS
Feed 1000 kg/h, 45 wt% acetone, 25 °CØ 0.40 m, 1.8 m active, 18 compartments
Solvent 350 kg/h TCE; target 10 wt% SFRotor discs Ø 0.24 m, 180 rpm
KD′​ = 1.85; tie lines, fig 6-65Drop-size and flooding constants
RDC ranges, tables 6-3 and 6-9Tanks, pumps, coolers, trips

Part 2 · summary

What Part 2 settled

  • TCE is dispersed: smaller volume flow, heavier, fed at the top.
  • Diameter comes from flooding (Thornton); design sits at 75 % of flooding.
  • Height = stages × HETS: 4.5 × 0.40 m = 1.8 m.
  • Rotor speed trades better transfer against flooding.

Part 3 · Operation

How do you keep the column on spec and away from flooding?

Part 3 · the plan

Running inside the operating window

  1. The operating envelopeflooding curve, operation curve and where the plant sits
  2. Four handlesrotor speed, feed, solvent ratio and temperature (book 6.7.3)
  3. Starting upcontinuous phase first, rotor before solvent, interface before ratio
  4. Shutting down and upsetssolvent before feed; what to cut first when it floods

Book fig 6-88

The operating envelope

Part 2 showed one flooding point. Repeat it for every feed rate and it becomes a curve.

  • Flooding curve: rotor speed that floods at each feed rate.
  • Operation curve: about 80 % of flooding, where the book advises running.
  • Above the curve drops are carried out; far below, extraction is poor.

Interactive · OTS model at S/F 0.35, 25 °C

Move the plant around its envelope

A feed increase at fixed speed walks the plant straight into flooding: raise feed only after lowering the rotor speed.

Book 6.7.3

Four handles and their price

RaiseHelps extraction byCosts you
Rotor speedsmaller drops, more areaflooding, emulsion, backmixing
Feed ratemore throughputflooding; more stages needed
Solvent ratiohigher extraction factormore TCE to recover
Temperaturehigher KD′​finer drops, dissolved TCE, vapour

Interactive · OTS model, one hour after each change

What each handle does to the raffinate

Only more solvent improves the spec without eating flooding margin: it is the safe handle, and the expensive one.

Choosing the temperature · book 6.3.2

Why the column runs at 25 °C

  • Warmer raises KD′​ about 1.7 % per °C.
  • But interfacial tension falls: finer drops, closer to flooding.
  • More TCE dissolves in the raffinate.
  • Acetone boils at 56 °C: TSHH-106 trips at 40 °C.

Chilled-water coolers E-101 and E-102 hold both inlets at 25 °C.

Starting up

Four rules behind the start-up order

The envelope says where to run. Start-up is how to get there without crossing it.

Continuous phase first

Fill and pressurise with feed.

Rotor before solvent

Drops must form, not jet.

Interface before ratio

Build it in MAN, then AUTO.

Speed up last

Raise rpm once flows are steady.

Interactive · the graded start-up procedure

Walk through the cold start-up

    The order protects the column: no solvent without drops, no ratio without a level to hold them.

    Shutting down

    Solvent off before feed

    1. Cut the feed to 600 kg/hratio stays on, solvent follows
    2. Slow the rotor to 120 rpmcoarser drops settle cleanly
    3. Stop solvent, then feednever solvent without a continuous phase
    4. Stop the rotor; LIC-109 to MAN, LV-109 shutthe interface is kept for the restart

    Upsets

    When the column starts to flood

    You seeBecause
    PDI-110 risingholdup builds in the active zone
    AI-113 risingTCE drops leave with the raffinate
    FI-115 fallingless solvent reaches the bottom

    Cut the rotor speed first, then the feed if that is not enough.

    Rules of thumb

    Seven operating rules

    • Continuous phase first.
    • Rotor before solvent; stay below 90 % of flooding.
    • Keep the interface at 35–65 %.
    • Stop solvent before feed.
    • Flooding: rotor first, feed next.
    • Check a lab sample before trimming solvent.
    • Change feed with the ratio on.

    Part 3 · summary

    What Part 3 settled

    • Run near 80 % of flooding: rotor speed and feed set the approach.
    • Solvent ratio is the safe but costly handle for the spec.
    • Start-up: feed, rotor, solvent, interface, ratio, then speed.
    • Flooding: PDI-110 and AI-113 up, FI-115 down; cut rpm first.

    Part 4 · Process description

    Where does every stream go, and what does it carry at design?

    Part 4 · the plan

    Following the acetone through the unit

    1. Block flow diagramsix numbered streams around C-101
    2. Feed and solvent sectionstanks, pumps, coolers and the ratio station
    3. The contactor and its two productsraffinate under pressure control, extract under interface control
    4. Balances at designwhere each kilogram of acetone, water and TCE ends up

    Interactive · click a stream number

    Block flow diagram

    Only two streams leave: everything that enters must turn up in the raffinate or the extract.

    Streams 1 and 2

    Feed section

    • Upstream fills feed tank T-101 through HIC-117.
    • P-101A runs; P-101B is the spare.
    • FIC-101 holds 1000 kg/h with FV-101.
    • Cooler E-101 takes the feed from 30 to 25 °C under TIC-102.
    • Feed enters the bottom of the active zone.

    Streams 3 and 4

    Solvent section

    • Recovered TCE returns from C-103 to drum D-102 at 38 °C.
    • P-102A runs; P-102B is the spare.
    • FFIC-103 keeps solvent at 0.35 × feed.
    • Cooler E-102 brings it to 25 °C under TIC-104.
    • The top distributor turns it into drops.

    Part 4 · summary

    What Part 4 settled

    • Feed 1000 kg/h in at the bottom; TCE 350 kg/h in at the top.
    • Raffinate 549 kg/h, 9 wt% acetone (SF), leaves the top under PIC-108.
    • Extract 801 kg/h, 50 wt% acetone, leaves the bottom under LIC-109.

    FFIC-103 in cascade (CAS)

    The solvent follows the feed

    Dashed: signals. The ratio R is the operator's handle; the feed sets the rest.

    Interactive · feed step with the ratio on or off

    What CAS mode buys you

    Ratio stationSP103​=R×F101​

    In AUTO the solvent stays at 350 kg/h after a feed change: S/F drifts and the spec is lost without anyone touching the solvent.

    LIC-109

    Holding the interface

    Ratio control fixes the inlets. The two outlets need their own loops.

    • Extract arriving raises the interface; LV-109 lets it out.
    • Direct acting: higher level, more opening.
    • Slow reset (240 s): the settler is a buffer, not a target.
    • Too low sends water to C-103; too high floods the active zone.

    Interactive · +20 % extract arriving at t = 1 min

    Tuning the interface controller

    Kc​
    controller gain
    %/%
    Ti​
    reset (integral) time
    s

    A fast reset makes the interface ring and LV-109 swing: averaging level control wants a gentle loop.

    PIC-108

    Pressure in a liquid-full column

    • No vapour space: pressure moves fast with any flow imbalance.
    • PV-108 on the raffinate: direct acting, fails open.
    • HV-108 bypass if PV-108 sticks.
    • PSHH-108 trips at 3.0 bar g; PSV-108 lifts at 3.5.

    Safety instrumented system

    Six interlocks

    No.CauseSettingAction
    I-1PSHH-108 pressure> 3.0 bar g, 3 sunit trip
    I-2TSHH-106 temperature> 40 °C, 10 sunit trip
    I-3LSLL-109 interface< 5 %, 5 sXV-119 closes
    I-4LSHH-109 interface> 95 %, 5 ssolvent pumps stop
    I-5LSLL-101 / 102 levels< 8 %, 3 stheir pumps stop
    I-6rotor overload> 3.0 kW, 10 srotor stops

    Interactive · click a cause

    Cause-and-effect matrix

    Only I-1, I-2 and the emergency shutdown (ESD) stop both flows: the other trips isolate one hazard and leave the rest running.

    Part 5 · summary

    What Part 5 settled

    • Seven loops; the solvent rides on the feed through FFIC-103.
    • Fail positions protect the column and C-103 on air failure.
    • LIC-109 is a gentle averaging loop; PIC-108 is fast.
    • Six interlocks; only pressure, temperature and ESD stop both flows.

    Alarms

    Alarm, acknowledge, act

    • One beep: new alarm. Two tones: a trip.
    • Silence stops sound; Acknowledge stops flashing.
    • Unacknowledged over 60 s costs score.
    • Most alarms only count while feeding.

    Part 6 · summary

    What Part 6 settled

    • Displays show; faceplates act. MAN sets OUT, AUTO sets SP, CAS sets R.
    • Colours tell service; square frames mark trip switches.
    • Acknowledge within 60 s; trend groups link cause and effect.
    • Field checks see what transmitters cannot.

    Outside the OTS boundary

    C-102 and C-103 depend on you

    C-102 raffinate stripper

    Strips dissolved TCE and leftover acetone from the water.

    Hurt by TCE drops (flooding).

    C-103 solvent recovery

    Boils acetone (56 °C) off TCE (114 °C); TCE returns to D-102.

    Hurt by water in the extract.

    Part 7 · summary

    What Part 7 settled

    • T-101 buys about 10 h; D-102 only about 2 h.
    • Pump and system curves set each flow; valves shape the system curve.
    • Coolers hold 25 °C only while chilled water stays cold.
    • C-102 needs a clear raffinate; C-103 needs a dry extract.

    Objectives first, then the situation

    1. How an exercise runsload, banner, faults on a schedule, grading

    What each procedure checks

    Steps tick themselves when the plant reaches them: order and safety count more than speed.

    Think EQUIPPED troubleshooting

    Six stages for a problem without a name

    1. Engage and Defineis it urgent? what, where, when, how much, what did not change
    2. Explorebalances, equilibrium, hydraulics, measurement: list hypotheses
    3. Plancheap tests that can fail: lab, stroboscope, sight glass
    4. Do it and Look backfix, compare with the prediction, stop it recurring

    Part 8 · summary

    What Part 8 settled

    • 18 training exercises, each one failure with a stated objective.
    • 7 graded procedures: safe, in order, on time, communicated.
    • 12 troubleshooting cases solved with the six stages.
    • The running score punishes off-spec, flooding and ignored alarms.

    To take away

    Key Takeaways

    1

    Use KD′​ and Kremser to know how many stages a target needs.

    2

    Run near 80 % of flooding; lower rotor speed before raising feed.

    3

    Keep solvent on ratio and the interface inside 35–65 %.

    4

    Cross-check any surprising reading with a balance or a field test.

    Before you open the OTS

    Exit tickets

    Which handle would you move first if AI-111 rose to 11 wt%, and why?

    2

    One reading on the DCS you would not trust without a field check.
